Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(Entertainment Weekly) -- It was a glass half-full, glass half-empty kind of weekend at the box office for "Funny People," writer-director Judd Apatow's comedic meditation on fame, humor, life, and death. Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen star in "Funny People," which took the No. 1 slot at the box office this weekend. According to figures from Hollywood.com Box Office, it opened at the top spot with an estimated $23.4 million, better than Apatow's The 40 Year-Old Virgin ($21.4 million) -- hence, the glass is half full. But that figure is far lower than the debut for Apatow's "Knocked Up" ($30.7 million), and it's the worst opening for a comedy for star Adam Sander since his 2000 turkey "Little Nicky" -- hence, the glass is half empty. Of course, "Funny People" was billed more as a thoughtful dramedy than a balls-out Sandler laugh-fest, and when matched against the opening frames for Sandler's serious efforts "Reign Over Me," "Spanglish," and "Punch-Drunk Love," Funny People is far and away the winner -- and the glass is half full again. But whether it's a comedy, drama, or dramedy, "Funny People's" $75 million budget is quite the handful of pretty pennies, and with a shaky "B-" Cinemascore, the film is going to have a hard time overcoming tepid word-of-mouth -- and we're back to the half-empty glass. So let's just move on, shall we? The cup of a certain adolescent wizard, meanwhile, definitely runneth over. Thanks to its debut on IMAX (and the premium ticket prices that come with it), "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" came in second with $17.7 million, a soft 40 percent drop from last weekend for $255.5 million total. At this rate, the film is well on its way to the upper ranks of the 'Potter' franchise. The guinea pigs of "G-Force" were right on its heels at third place, nibbling up $17.1 million, a decent 46 percent drop for a two-week cume of $66.5 million. And Katherine Heigl's romcom "The Ugly Truth" took in an additional $13 million, a 53 percent drop for fourth place and $54.5 million total. Of the two other wide releases this weekend, at least the sci-fi family comedy "Aliens in the Attic" -- which grossed a meager $7.8 million for fifth place -- broke into the top 10. The torture porn flick "The Collector" collected a grisly $3.6 million and plopped dead at 11th place. Box office on a whole was down a massive 22 percent from last year, when The "Dark Knight" and "The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor" both took in over $40 million, but the specialty market showed some vibrant signs of life. Bone fide indie hit "(500) Days of Summer" expanded to 266 theaters for $2.7 million, a $10,338 per theater average. And three widely disparate films opened in four theaters each to healthy per theater averages: The quirky romantic comedy "Adam" ($16,566 per theater), the stylish vampire film "Thirst" ($13,793 per theater), and the eco-thriller-cum-documentary "The Cove" ($13,600 per theater). Finally, a true milestone was reached this weekend by "The Hangover." With $5.1 million this weekend for a running total of $255.8 million, the summer's biggest die hard blockbuster has passed "Star Trek" and (for a brief moment) "Harry Potter 6" as the third highest grossing movie of the year. Hollywood.com Box Office reported an opening weekend haul of approximately $23.4 million—surpassing Apatow's earlier hit "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" (which debuted at $21.4 million). That's the optimistic take. On the flip side, this number falls well short of the $30.7 million opening that Apatow's "Knocked Up" achieved, and it represents Sandler's weakest comedy debut since 2000's critically panned "Little Nicky." That's the pessimistic view.

Granted, "Funny People" was marketed as a more introspective dramedy rather than pure Sandler slapstick. Compared to the openings of Sandler's dramatic films like "Reign Over Me," "Spanglish," and "Punch-Drunk Love," this film performed considerably better—swinging the pendulum back toward optimism. Yet with a substantial $75 million production budget and a mediocre "B-" grade on Cinemascore, the movie may struggle against lukewarm audience buzz, tilting things back toward pessimism once more. Let's move forward.

Meanwhile, things looked considerably brighter for a certain teenage wizard. Boosted by its IMAX release (complete with premium pricing), "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" landed in second place with $17.7 million—only a modest 40 percent decline from its opening weekend—bringing its cumulative total to $255.5 million. The franchise appears poised to climb toward the top tier of Potter films.

Close behind, animated rodents "G-Force" secured third place, earning $17.1 million (a reasonable 46 percent drop) for a two-week total of $66.5 million. Among the weekend's two remaining wide releases, "Aliens in the Attic" managed to crack the top ten despite a modest $7.8 million fifth-place finish. The horror film "The Collector" fared worse, limping to $3.6 million and an 11th-place ranking.

Overall industry revenue dropped sharply—22 percent below last year's comparable weekend, when both "The Dark Knight" and "The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor" each exceeded $40 million. # Box Office Report: "Funny People" Tops Charts Amid Mixed Signals

Judd Apatow's latest comedy, "Funny People," claimed the No. 1 spot at the weekend box office, pulling in an estimated $23.4 million. The film, which stars Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen in a story blending comedy with dramatic undertones about mortality and fame, outperformed Apatow's earlier hit "The 40 Year-Old Virgin" but fell short of matching the opening success of his 2007 blockbuster "Knocked Up." This places "Funny People" in a middle tier among Apatow's directorial efforts, suggesting audiences responded positively but not overwhelmingly to the film's darker comedic tone.

## A Complicated Debut for Sandler

While the No. 1 ranking might suggest an unqualified success, a closer look at the numbers reveals some concerning signs for star Adam Sandler. This opening weekend actually represents his weakest debut for a comedy since 2000's poorly received "Little Nicky," a notable statistic given Sandler's typically strong track record in the genre. However, there's a silver lining: the film still managed to outperform Sandler's more dramatic ventures, including "Reign Over Me" and "Spanglish," indicating that audiences remain more receptive to him in comedic roles, even when those comedies venture into more serious territory.

## Warning Signs for Long-Term Performance

Despite claiming the top spot, "Funny People" faces significant challenges ahead. The film carries a hefty $75 million production budget, meaning it will need sustained box office performance to reach profitability. Compounding this concern is the film's lukewarm "B-" Cinemascore rating—a metric that measures audience satisfaction immediately after viewing. This middling grade suggests that word-of-mouth, often crucial for a film's staying power in theaters, may not provide the boost "Funny People" needs to maintain momentum in the coming weeks. Industry analysts will be watching closely to see whether the film can defy these early warning signs.

## Harry Potter Continues Strong Run

Securing second place, "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" added $17.7 million to its impressive domestic haul, pushing its cumulative total to $255.5 million. The film's continued strength at the box office has been notably bolstered by premium IMAX pricing, which allows theaters to charge higher ticket prices for the enhanced viewing experience. This strategy has proven effective in maximizing revenue even as the film moves into its later weeks of release, demonstrating the growing importance of premium formats in sustaining blockbuster earnings.

## Rounding Out the Top Five

The remainder of the top box office positions saw notable weekend-over-weekend declines. "G-Force," the Jerry Bruckheimer-produced spy comedy featuring computer-animated guinea pigs, claimed third place with $17.1 million. Meanwhile, the romantic comedy "The Ugly Truth," starring Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler, rounded out the notable performers with $13 million. Both films experienced substantial drop-offs from their previous weekend numbers, a common pattern for films entering their second or third weeks of release as initial audience enthusiasm wanes and new releases capture public attention.

# "Funny People" Debuts at No. 1, But Can It Hold the Crown?

Judd Apatow's latest comedy-drama hybrid, "Funny People," opened at the top of the box office this weekend, pulling in an estimated $23.4 million across theaters nationwide. The film, which reunites Apatow with frequent collaborators Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen, marks another notch in the director's growing filmography of R-rated comedies that blend raunchy humor with genuine emotional depth.

The opening numbers place "Funny People" in an interesting middle ground within Apatow's directorial output. The debut comfortably surpassed the $19.4 million opening of "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" back in 2005, suggesting that Apatow's brand has grown stronger with audiences over the past several years. However, it fell noticeably short of the $30.7 million debut posted by "Knocked Up" in 2007, indicating that while the Apatow name still carries weight, this particular film may not have captured the same broad audience enthusiasm as his previous hit.

For star Adam Sandler, the opening represents something of a cautionary data point. Despite his standing as one of Hollywood's most bankable comedic leads, this $23.4 million debut stands as his weakest opening for a comedy since 2000's critically panned "Little Nicky," which opened to $16.2 million on its way to a disappointing overall run. The comparison is notable given that Sandler's comedies have typically opened in the $30-40 million range or higher in recent years, making this relatively modest start a point of discussion among industry analysts.

Meanwhile, holding steady in the No. 2 position was "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince," which added another $17.7 million in its third weekend of release. The wizarding franchise entry has shown remarkable staying power, and much of its continued strength can be attributed to its IMAX presentation, which has allowed the film to command premium ticket prices and draw repeat business from fans eager to experience the film's visual spectacle on the largest screens available. The IMAX factor has become an increasingly important tool for tentpole releases looking to extend their theatrical shelf life.

While a $23.4 million opening might read as underwhelming for a film featuring two major comedic stars, industry observers note that the number is actually quite respectable when considering "Funny People's" hybrid dramedy structure. Unlike Apatow's previous directorial efforts, which leaned more heavily into straightforward comedy, "Funny People" tackles weightier themes involving mortality and personal redemption, wrapped in Apatow's signature blend of crude humor and heart. For a film that doesn't fit neatly into the typical summer comedy mold, the opening weekend performance suggests audiences were willing to give the unconventional structure a chance, at least initially.

That said, several red flags are emerging that could complicate the film's path to profitability. Chief among these is the film's substantial $75 million production budget—a hefty price tag for what is fundamentally a character-driven comedy-drama rather than an effects-laden blockbuster. Recouping that investment, along with marketing costs, will require the film to demonstrate strong legs in the coming weeks rather than a rapid decline typical of front-loaded openings.

Compounding these concerns is the film's "B-" CinemaScore rating, a metric that surveys opening-night audiences on their satisfaction with the film they just watched. A "B-" grade, while not disastrous, falls short of the "A" or "A-" ratings that typically correlate with strong word-of-mouth and sustained box office performance through positive audience buzz. Comedies in particular tend to rely heavily on repeat viewership and enthusiastic recommendations from friends and family, making tepid audience reception a potential warning sign for the weeks ahead.

Industry analysts will be watching closely to see how "Funny People" performs in its second weekend, as the combination of a lukewarm CinemaScore and a budget that demands strong sustained performance creates uncertainty about whether the film can achieve the kind of box office longevity that made "Knocked Up" such a success story two years prior. Should word-of-mouth fail to improve or audience interest wane quickly, the film may struggle to justify its substantial budget despite its solid opening weekend showing.

# Entertainment Weekly: The Lighter Side of Pop Culture

For decades, Entertainment Weekly has served as a trusted guide to the world of movies, television, music, and celebrity culture. But beyond its reviews and rankings, the magazine has built a reputation for something equally valuable: its ability to be genuinely funny.

## Wit as a Signature Style

What sets Entertainment Weekly apart from other publications covering the same beat is its willingness not to take itself too seriously. Writers often sneak clever jokes into their reviews, headlines play with puns, and even serious critiques carry a light touch that makes reading about pop culture feel like chatting with a witty friend rather than consulting an academic journal.

This humor serves an important purpose. Entertainment, after all, is meant to bring joy, and a magazine covering that world benefits from reflecting that same spirit back to its readers. Whether it's a snarky comment about a celebrity's questionable fashion choice or a tongue-in-cheek ranking of the "worst movie sequels ever made," the funny commentary keeps readers engaged and entertained even when the actual content being reviewed might be mediocre.

## Finding Comedy in Criticism

One of the magazine's greatest strengths lies in how it handles negative reviews. Rather than delivering harsh critiques, EW writers often find humor in a film's failures or a show's missteps. This approach makes even bad reviews enjoyable to read, turning potential disappointment into comedic material that readers can laugh along with rather than feel discouraged by.

## A Weekly Dose of Fun

The "Weekly" aspect of the publication means readers get a regular, reliable source of both information and amusement. This consistency has helped build a loyal readership who look forward not just to learning about the latest celebrity gossip or box office numbers, but to enjoying the clever, often laugh-out-loud writing style that has become the magazine's trademark.

In an industry that can sometimes feel oversaturated with serious analysis, Entertainment Weekly's commitment to humor reminds us that covering entertainment should, above all, be entertaining itself.

# 'Half-Blood Prince' Casts Spell Over Box Office, But Sandler's 'Funny People' Struggles to Get Last Laugh

**By EW Staff**

Harry Potter proved once again that magic sells, as *Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince* continued its dominance at the box office, though Judd Apatow's *Funny People* couldn't quite conjure the numbers Universal was hoping for in its opening weekend.

**HARRY POTTER AND THE HALF-BLOOD PRINCE**
Warner Bros.' sixth installment in the boy wizard franchise continued its box office magic, adding another $31.2 million in its second weekend for a domestic total of $203.8 million. The film, which shattered records with its $158 million opening, has already crossed $400 million worldwide, proving that even in a crowded summer marketplace, audiences can't resist a trip back to Hogwarts.

**FUNNY PEOPLE**
Adam Sandler's dramedy about a dying comedian opened to a middling $22.7 million, a soft number for a film that cost a reported $75 million to make and paired Sandler with Apatow's signature blend of raunch and sentiment. Critics were divided on the nearly two-and-a-half-hour running time, and audiences seemed similarly split—the film earned a "B" CinemaScore, suggesting the mix of dick jokes and cancer drama proved a tricky sell. Co-stars Seth Rogen, Jonah Hill, and Jason Schwartzman couldn't quite juice the numbers into blockbuster territory.

**G-FORCE**
Disney's guinea pig spy caper held up respectably in its second weekend, nabbing $17.3 million and bringing its domestic haul to $58.9 million. Proof that talking rodents with tiny sunglasses remain a surprisingly durable commodity for family audiences.

**THE UGLY TRUTH**
The Katherine Heigl-Gerard Butler rom-com continued its solid run, pulling in $11.3 million in its third weekend for a cumulative $63.1 million—a reminder that counterprogramming against the boys' club of summer blockbusters can still pay off.

**ORPHAN**
Warner Bros.' creepy-kid thriller slashed its way to a decent $9 million in its second weekend, bringing its total to $32.4 million, as horror fans continued to whisper "there's something wrong with Esther" to anyone who'd listen.

**THE BOTTOM LINE**
While *Half-Blood Prince* remains the summer's undisputed heavyweight, *Funny People*'s soft debut raises questions about whether Apatow's more introspective, R-rated approach—complete with meditations on mortality—was simply too much of a tonal shift for audiences expecting another *Knocked Up*. Still, with a reported budget in the $75 million range, the film will need strong holds and overseas numbers to reach profitability. Meanwhile, Harry Potter shows no signs of loosening his grip on multiplexes anytime soon.

# Weekend Box Office Report: 'Funny People' Draws Laughs, But Not Crowds

**Judd Apatow's Star-Studded Dramedy Opens Below Expectations as 'G.I. Joe' Holds Strong**

This weekend's box office saw Universal's "Funny People," starring Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen, debut in the top spot but with softer numbers than the star power might have suggested, while holdovers showed the durability of late-summer counterprogramming.

## Top 10 Domestic Box Office

**1. Funny People** — $23.4 million (Opening Weekend)
Judd Apatow's follow-up to "Knocked Up" and "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" opened to a muted debut for a film with this much star wattage—Sandler, Rogen, Leslie Mann, and a scene-stealing Eric Bana. The R-rated dramedy about a famous comedian facing his mortality struggled with a bloated 146-minute runtime and tonal shifts that divided critics and audiences alike. Despite a "B+" CinemaScore, the $75 million-budgeted film opened below the openings of Apatow's previous directorial efforts.

**2. G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra** — $18.9 million (-52%)
Paramount's toy-based action tentpole continued its assault on the box office in week two, with Channing Tatum and Sienna Miller's franchise-starter proving it has legs despite so-so reviews. **3. District 9** — $15.5 million (-31%)
Neill Blomkamp's inventive sci-fi allegory, produced by Peter Jackson, continues to overperform relative to its modest budget, holding well in its sophomore frame. Word-of-mouth and strong reviews are fueling this sleeper's momentum.

**5. G-Force** — $6.8 million (-38%)
Disney's Jerry Bruckheimer-produced guinea pig spy comedy remains a steady performer with family audiences amid a competitive summer family-film landscape.

**6. Julie & Julia** — $6.7 million (-27%)
Meryl Streep's Julia Child continues to charm upscale audiences, with the Nora Ephron-directed foodie favorite showing exceptional legs as it expands into more theaters.

**7. The Ugly Truth** — $4.1 million (-40%)
The Katherine Heigl/Gerard Butler rom-com continues its steady descent after weeks in the top five.

**8. Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince** — $3.9 million (-45%)
Warner Bros.' blockbuster wizard adventure continues its marathon run, closing in on $275 million domestically after weeks atop the charts.

**9. Orphan** — $3.6 million (-52%)
The creepy-kid horror thriller drops as expected in its third weekend but has already cleared its modest budget many times over.

**10. (500) Days of Summer** — $3.2 million (-18%)
Fox Searchlight's indie darling continues its patient expansion strategy, holding remarkably well as it rolls out to additional markets on the strength of glowing reviews and word-of-mouth for Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel.

---

### The Takeaway

While "Funny People" claimed the top spot, industry watchers noted the film's opening fell short of the roughly $30+ million many predicted given its cast and Apatow's pedigree—suggesting either dramedy fatigue or audience hesitance toward the film's heavier subject matter and lengthy runtime. Joe" proved surprisingly durable, and "District 9" continued to demonstrate that original, well-reviewed genre fare can still find an audience in a marketplace dominated by sequels and adaptations. With August underway, studios will be watching closely to see whether "Funny People" can find legs via reviews and word-of-mouth, or whether it settles in as one of the more disappointing outputs from the Apatow comedy machine.

# Funny People's Box Office Debut: A Tale of Mixed Expectations

**A $23.4 Million Weekend That Left Hollywood Divided**

When Judd Apatow's "Funny People" hit theaters, its opening weekend haul of roughly $23 million presented an unusual case study in how context shapes perception in Hollywood. The film wasn't a flop by conventional standards—it topped the box office—but for a movie carrying Apatow's name and starring Adam Sandler alongside rising comedy star Seth Rogen, the number sparked immediate industry debate.

## The Apatow Standard

The comparison to "Knocked Up" proved unavoidable and, in many ways, unfair. That 2007 sleeper hit opened to $30.7 million and went on to gross over $148 million domestically, becoming a cultural touchstone that redefined mainstream comedy. "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" similarly overperformed, opening to $21.4 million against a modest budget before legging out to nearly $110 million.

"Funny People" arrived with a considerably larger budget—reportedly north of $75 million, dwarfing its predecessors—and higher built-in expectations given Apatow's now-established brand as a hitmaker. When a film costs more but opens to comparable or lesser numbers than movies that cost half as much, the math becomes a talking point regardless of the film's actual quality.

## The Sandler Factor

Adam Sandler's involvement added another layer of complexity. Sandler's comedies have historically been opening-weekend juggernauts—"Little Nicky," despite becoming something of a punchline critically, still managed a $17.5 million opening in 2000 on the strength of Sandler's box office draw alone, an amount considered underwhelming *for Sandler* at the time despite outpacing many comedies of that era.

The fact that "Funny People"—a film more ambitious and dramatically weighted than typical Sandler fare—opened in the same general neighborhood as one of his more maligned efforts raised eyebrows. Sandler's core audience, conditioned to expect broad, high-energy comedies like "Big Daddy" or "Happy Gilmore," seemed hesitant about a film blending stand-up comedy culture with meditations on mortality and regret.

## Reading Between the Numbers

Industry analysts pointed to several factors muddying the "success or disappointment" narrative:

**The Genre-Bending Problem**: "Funny People" was marketed as a comedy but functioned substantially as a dramedy about a famous comedian (Sandler) confronting a serious illness. This tonal ambiguity likely affected the casual moviegoer turnout that had made "Knocked Up" such explosive counter-programming.

**Running Time and Repeat Viewing**: At nearly two and a half hours, the film's length worked against the kind of multiple-viewing pattern that helped "Knocked Up" build its legs through summer 2007.

**Rogen's Evolving Star Power**: Having Rogen as co-lead invited direct comparison to his previous starring vehicle, yet audiences may have been experiencing early signs of Rogen fatigue after his rapid ascension through "Knocked Up," "Superbad," and "Pineapple Express."

## The Verdict: Success Through a Different Lens

Ultimately, "Funny People's" opening represented what industry observers might call a "prestige comedy" performance rather than a blockbuster one. It succeeded in opening at number one and validating Apatow's ability to greenlight ambitious, personal projects with A-list talent. Yet compared to the explosive, word-of-mouth-driven trajectories of "Knocked Up" and "The 40-Year-Old Virgin"—films that started reasonably and multiplied through cultural buzz—"Funny People" faced the harder task of justifying its budget against a more modest ceiling.

The film became less a referendum on Apatow's talent and more a case study in how audience expectations, shaped by a filmmaker's previous successes, can transform a solid opening into a discussion of underperformance—proving that in Hollywood, context isn't just important; sometimes it's everything.

# Box Office Report: Apatow's 'People' Underwhelms While Potter Keeps Casting His Spell

This weekend proved that even comedy's reigning king can have an off night. Judd Apatow's "Funny People," starring Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen, opened to a so-so $23.4 million, a notably softer debut than Apatow's previous directorial efforts "Knocked Up" ($30.7 million) and "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" ($21.4 million, though that one built over time rather than front-loading). Despite strong reviews and a starry cast that included Leslie Mann, Eric Bana, and a parade of comedy cameos, audiences seemed hesitant to embrace a film that mixes big laughs with meditations on mortality. At two and a half hours, "Funny People" also faced natural attrition from multiple daily showings—something distributor Universal surely anticipated but perhaps not to this degree.

"We knew this was a movie that would generate discussion," said a Universal distribution executive, choosing his words carefully. "It's not a straight comedy, and we think it'll have legs as word of mouth spreads about what Judd's really doing here."

Meanwhile, in its third week of release, "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" continues to prove that wizarding wins wide. The Warner Bros. tentpole added another $22.3 million, pushing its domestic total past $255 million and its worldwide haul north of $650 million. With little in the way of family-friendly competition until "G-Force" arrived, Potter has had the multiplex largely to himself for weeks—a luxury that's paying dividends deep into the summer.

Speaking of "G-Force," Disney's guinea-pig spy caper (produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, because apparently rodents need action-movie pedigree too) opened respectably if unspectacularly with $32.2 million. Kids clearly wanted their talking-animal fix, even if critics were less than enthusiastic about the Nicolas Cage-produced adventure. The film's 3-D presentations helped pad the numbers, with premium pricing doing what premium pricing does.

Rounding out the weekend's wide releases, "The Ugly Truth" continued its surprisingly sturdy run. The Katherine Heigl-Gerard Butler rom-com, which opened two weeks ago to $27 million, has proven that raunchy date-night comedies still have an audience, especially when Heigl brings her established fan base and Butler brings, well, his abs. The film has now crossed $60 million domestically, a solid result for a film that cost a reported $38 million.

**On the specialty side**, two films continued their slow-and-steady climb toward crossover success. Marc Webb's "(500) Days of Summer," the Zooey Deschanel-Joseph Gordon-Levitt indie darling that's been charming urban audiences since its limited July 17 debut, expanded into more theaters and posted encouraging per-screen averages. Fox Searchlight has been platforming the film carefully, banking on positive buzz (and Deschanel's undeniable "it girl" status) to fuel an old-fashioned slow burn into late summer counterprogramming success.

Also generating heat: "The Cove," Louie Psihoyos' documentary about dolphin hunting in Japan, which opened in limited release to strong numbers and even stronger discussion. The film, produced with backing from the Oceanic Preservation Society, has drawn comparisons to "An Inconvenient Truth" for its ability to turn environmental advocacy into thriller-paced entertainment. Expect awards-season chatter to follow as Roadside Attractions expands the film's footprint.

**The bottom line:** Summer 2009 continues to prove that audiences will show up for franchise reliability (Potter), family diversion (G-Force), and comfort-food comedy (Ugly Truth), while giving more challenging fare (Funny People) a slightly cooler reception than its pedigree might have suggested. Meanwhile, the specialty market keeps chugging along, proving there's still room at the multiplex for movies that don't come with built-in merchandising opportunities.

Next week brings "Julie & Julia," which will test whether Meryl Streep doing a Julia Child impression can lure counter-programming crowds away from... well, probably more Harry Potter, if we're being honest.
